Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it

I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' directly conflicts with 'When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop.' Those two states can sometimes fluctuate, but as selected core items they describe opposing levels of accessibility/distress and are not clinically coherent without further qualification.

vignette: Malik’s first memory of the night he was assaulted is as sharp and sudden as the thud of a baseball: a glass bottle swung from a drunken hand, splattering in the alley, the air filled with the acrid scent of spilled beer. The sound of that impact still sends his heart racing, and when he hears an object being thrown—whether a paper bag kicked across a parking lot or a door slamming in a conference room—he feels the same rush of terror he felt then, as though the past were erupting again. The mere sight of an angry face, even if the expression is calm, reminds him of the man’s clenched fists and makes him freeze. And the scent of alcohol on a bartender’s breath or a gym locker becomes a trigger that pulls him back into that night, a sensory reminder of a time when he felt powerless. These triggers do not merely flash memories; they pull Malik into a web of self‑blame. Whenever he is confronted with an angry tone, he finds himself replaying the assault in his mind, ruminating on what he might have done differently, and blaming himself for not resisting. He also begins to gamble, a frantic attempt to recapture the fleeting adrenaline of that night, to feel a pulse of control even if it is only a thin veil. Avoiding any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation becomes a way to keep the world from bringing him back to the scene, to stay away from anyone who might threaten him. Thus, the triggers set in motion his maladaptive strategies, and these strategies, in turn, keep him locked in a cycle of avoidance. The startle to ordinary sounds that once seemed benign—traffic, a siren, even a phone vibrating on a desk—now feel like the prelude to another attack. Unexpected movement, such as a colleague’s abrupt stride toward him, sends him leaping, as if his body has forgotten how to stay still. Even when a coworker reassures him that the city’s streets are safe, Malik cannot trust that reassurance; the memory of the assault has eroded his sense of safety, making him think that danger can lurk wherever he goes. This persistent threat keeps his body on edge, ready to react to any perceived danger, and fuels his gambling and self‑blame. The sense of threat itself, rooted in the memory of being struck, feeds back into the memory: every time he is startled, he relives that night in vivid snapshots, the same split‑second images flickering in his mind. These images overwhelm him so much that he often stops speaking, unable to find words that could explain the terror he feels. When Malik finally speaks to a friend about the assault, he can describe what happened but cannot find the right words. The inability to articulate the event only heightens his sense of helplessness: he feels that no one can understand his pain, that the institutions meant to protect him—police, the courthouse, even his own university—failed him. He interprets that failure as a personal loss of coping power: he believes he cannot even manage the slightest upset. These negative appraisals feed into his threat perception: if the world and its safeguards are unreliable, the likelihood of another assault is always on his mind. The feeling of helplessness also pushes him deeper into his self‑blame ruminations, making the cycle tighter. Malik’s gambling becomes both a response to the threat and a way to distract from the memory. Each spin of a roulette wheel, each card dealt, is a brief moment of release from the relentless startle responses that otherwise dominate his day. Yet, the more he plays, the more he finds himself returning to the memory of that night, and the more he can’t find the words to describe the event. The avoidance of conflict, too, keeps him from confronting the institutions that let him down, thereby preserving his sense that the world is unfair and dangerous. His urban planning work, a field that relies on precision and collaboration, feels increasingly alien: he can no longer focus on zoning maps or community meetings because the threat of confrontation is always lurking, his mind replaying the assault every time he hears a heated debate or a sudden noise. The loop grew tighter over weeks and months. He avoided social gatherings, turned down promotions that required teamwork, and found himself isolated in the apartment where the only sound that calmed him was the steady hum of his own breathing. Each time a friend offered reassurance about his safety, Malik’s disbelief was a testament to the lasting impact of the assault. When he finally decided to seek help, it was because the gambling had begun to interfere with his finances, his job performance had slipped, and the constant anxiety had started to feel like a prison he could no longer escape from. Malik is now afraid that the fear will never fade and hopeful that a therapist can help him untangle the loop that keeps him bound to the night in the alley, allowing him to rebuild trust in both himself and the world around him.
